title: Perf Signal → Source Mapping Guide
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, pragmatic working guide for mapping an observed performance signal (SLO miss, latency spike, throughput drop, increased tail p99/p999) to likely subsystem sources. Aim: speed up first-60-minutes triage, reduce noisy blames, and provide repeatable bisect & canary comparison heuristics.

Audience:
- on-call SREs
- serving-runtime engineers debugging regressions
- release leads validating canaries

How to use:
- Start at the top: classify signal type, magnitude, and scope.
- Run the quick checklist (Section A).
- Use the mapping table (Section B) to focus measurements.
- If noisy or intermittent, use bisect heuristics (Section D).

A. Quick checklist (first 10–20 minutes)
- Scope: single node / pool / region / global? (check routing logs + autoscaler events)
- Magnitude: relative increase vs baseline (percent delta) and absolute (ms / tokens/sec)
- User impact: latency p50/p95/p99? Error rate change? Time window of onset?
- Canary vs prod: was a rollout happening? which model/version changed?
- Resource pressure: GPU util, CPU steal, host loadavg, memory usage, disk IO, NIC saturation
- Configs changed: batching params, kernel flags, quantization profile, runtime flags (from rollout commits)
- Recent infra changes: kernel/driver updates, CUDA, container runtime, instance type changes

B. Signal → Likely source mapping (fast heuristics)
- Increased average latency, uniform across requests: likely global batching/pacing change, queuing config, or autoscaler scaling down pools.
- Increased tail latency (p99/p999) without avg rising much: KV cache thrash, cold cache effects, GC/paging, GPU kernel slowdown on long sequences, scheduler starvation.
- Throughput drop but latency similar: throughput cap (burst policy exhausted), tokenization hotpath, network egress throttling, host-level cgroup limits.
- Error spike + latency rise: model OOM or runtime crash causing retries, or miscompiled kernel causing invalid fp ops and retries.
- Increased variance correlated to request size distribution: batching strategy mismatch—batches growing and causing head-of-line latency.
- Sudden step-change at deploy time: model variant mismatch, changed quantization matrix, or a change in request routing policy.

C. Dashboard quick-probes (ordered)
1) Overview: global latency heatmap + request volume by region/model/version (time window: 15m/1h/6h).
   - Panels to open: per-route p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, errors/sec.
2) Host/GPU health: GPU util %, GPU memory used, GPU mem alloc failures, CPU steal, host loadavg, dmesg/syslog errors (OOM killer).
3) Queue/backlog: request queue length per worker, average batch size over time, batch wait time histogram.
4) KV cache metrics: hit rate (prefix), eviction rate, KV cache size.
5) Kernel/exec metrics: per-op latency breakdown if available (attention, matmul, softmax), kernel retries/slow-path counts.
6) Network/disk: NIC TX/RX, disk latency useful for disk-backed caches.
7) GC/alloc: host/container memory alloc latency, swap usage, page faults/sec.

D. Canary comparison + bisect strategy
- Canary diff approach:
  1) Compare equivalent panels for canary cohort vs baseline cohort over aligned windows (same RPS/baseline traffic).
  2) Important: normalize by request size and model version. If canary sees larger average sequence length, differences are expected.
  3) Use ratios not absolute deltas for p99 (p99_canary / p99_base). Thresholds: >1.15 for p95, >1.25 for p99 triggers deeper triage.
- Bisect heuristics (if deploy suspected):
  1) Start with the commit window between last-good and first-bad deploy. Split in half and reproduce with controlled load in staging (use same model files and quantization).
  2) Prioritize commits that touch: batching, kernel selection, allocator, model compilation, numpy/torch ops.
  3) If bisect is noisy, run repeated runs (N=5) and compare distributions (use percentile bootstrap).

E. Profiling recipes (fast, minimal disruption)
- GPU quick: collect per-request timelines using lightweight tracing (runtime-level op timestamps). If op-level not available, sample with nvprof/cupti for 1–2 minutes on a single worker on replicated traffic.
  - Command (example): nvprof --profile-from-start off --export-profile profile.nvvp --duration 120 <repro-binary> (run on debug instance)
- CPU quick: perf record -g -F 99 -p <pid> -- sleep 60 ; perf script | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg
- Python-level hotspots: run py-spy top for 30s on worker to see interpreter hotspots (cheap, no restart).
- Memory/alloc: enable jemalloc stats (if used), or run heap profiling for Python process. Look for growth across requests.
- KV cache tracing: instrument cache lookup/insert latency for a sampled 1% of requests and dump to file for histogram analysis.

F. Repro microbench checklist
- Reproduce traffic shape: request size distribution, sequence length histogram, batch arrival pattern. Use existing loadgen scripts (locust or internal loadgen).
- Run with and without cache warmup to test cache sensitivity.
- Run single-node debug with identical GPU driver/kernel to rule out infra.
- Toggle suspect flags (quantize on/off, new kernel selection) to isolate delta.

G. Example investigation timeline (first 3 hours)
- 0–10m: classify scope, severity, open incident, note baseline.
- 10–30m: basic dashboard probes (Section C), collect logs and top metrics.
- 30–60m: targeted lightweight profiling (Section E), run canary vs baseline comparisons.
- 60–120m: reproduce in staging or on a debug instance; start bisect if deploy window small.
- 120–180m: root cause hypothesis, mitigation (rollback, autoscaler tweak, fallback variant) and postmortem stub.

H. Common false-positives and traps
- Misattributing p99 increases to model change when caused by traffic mix shift (longer prompts). Always compare normalized by length.
- Treating GPU util drop as harmless — sometimes low util is caused by long kernel stalls; correlate with per-op latencies.
- Ignoring OS-level driver logs — kernel messages often show NV driver timeouts, which are severe.

I. Quick mitigations (triage-stage)
- Route to older model variant or fallback pool for immediate mitigation.
- Throttle request admission (reduce RPS) to restore SLO while triage proceeds.
- Increase batching timeout to reduce head-of-line if small-request flood causing tiny batches (trade-off increased avg latency).

J. Notes / TODOs (work-in-progress)
- Add canned Grafana dashboard JSON snippets for the panels in Section C.
- Build a short script to compute normalized p99 ratios across canary vs baseline cohorts.
- Automate KV cache sampling for production traffic when p99 drift > 10%.
- Investigate adding lightweight op-level instrumentation by default in canaries.

Unresolved questions:
- How to cheaply collect per-op GPU latency at scale without heavy nvprof overhead?
- What statistical test threshold do we standardize on for auto-alerting from canary diffs? (A/B test vs percentile bootstrap)

References and quick links:
- Internal dashboards: grafana.redwood/serving/runtime/overview (placeholder)
- Perf playbook (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/PerfPlaybook
- Bisect helper script: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tools/bisect-helper
